subject: physiology
title: Poiseuille Law, Vascular Resistance, and Turbulent Flow

steps.tx: The steady laminar flow of a viscous fluid through a rigid cylindrical tube is formulated by the Hagen-Poiseuille relationship, known as **Poiseuille law**. Volume flow rate is directly proportional to the pressure gradient and the fourth power of vessel internal radius, and inversely proportional to fluid viscosity and vessel length.
steps.say: Poiseuille law dictates that volume flow rate is proportional to the fourth power of vessel radius and inversely proportional to viscosity and length.

nodes.label: Arteriolar Radius (r) Doubles: 2 to the 4th Power = 16-Fold Rise
Vascular Blood Flow Surges 16-Fold at Identical Driving Pressure
Conversely, Vascular Resistance Plummets to 1/16th of Baseline
Small Caliber Changes Strongly Control Organ Perfusion

steps.tx: Because radius is raised to the fourth power, minute changes in arteriolar caliber exert profound effects on **vascular resistance**. Arterioles possess thick circular muscular media richly innervated by sympathetic noradrenergic fibres, accounting for over sixty percent of total systemic peripheral vascular resistance and acting as the primary stopcocks regulating tissue perfusion.
steps.say: Because radius is raised to the fourth power, arterioles act as resistance stopcocks, where minor caliber changes control peripheral vascular resistance.

rows: Primary site of systemic vascular resistance

steps.tx: Blood in large vessels does not flow as a stirred soup but as silent layers. **Laminar flow** stacks concentric laminae fastest at the centre and still at the wall, which keeps resistance predictable under Poiseuille physics. When velocity or vessel geometry breaks that order, turbulence wastes energy and makes murmurs and bruits audible. The quiet of normal flow is therefore diagnostic information delivered free at every auscultation.
steps.say: Laminar flow layers blood fastest at the centre and still at the wall. Turbulence wastes energy and creates murmurs and bruits.

vis.alt: Image showing laminar flow with concentric layers inside a blood vessel.
vis.caption: Concentric layers of blood slide fastest at the centre of a vessel. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: In smooth, unobstructed cylindrical vessels, blood moves in concentric concentric fluid laminae, designated **laminar flow**. Fluid layers in the central axial stream move at maximal velocity, while velocity drops parabolically toward the vascular wall, where fluid remains stationary due to viscous friction, minimizing energy dissipation and preventing audible vascular murmurs.
steps.say: In laminar flow, concentric blood layers move smoothly without turbulence. Central axial flow travels fastest while wall friction creates a parabolic profile.

vis.alt: Laminar versus turbulent microvascular blood flow.
vis.caption: Parabolic velocity profile of laminar blood flow in peripheral microvessels. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: When flow velocity exceeds a critical threshold, streamline organisation disintegrates into chaotic vortices and eddies termed **turbulent flow**. Turbulence dissipates kinetic energy into acoustic vibrations and heat, producing audible murmurs across stenotic cardiac valves, vascular bruits over atherosclerotic carotids, and Korotkoff sounds during sphygmomanometric blood pressure cuff deflation.
steps.say: Turbulent flow occurs when streamlines break down into chaotic eddies, producing audible murmurs across stenotic valves and arterial bruits.

left.title: Laminar (Streamline) Flow
points: Concentric cylindrical fluid layers slide silently
Parabolic velocity profile across vessel lumen
Pressure gradient is directly proportional to flow (P ~ Q)
Minimizes shear stress and energetic pumping cost

right.title: Turbulent Flow
points: Blunt velocity profile with high wall shear stress
Pressure gradient increases with square of flow (P ~ Q^2)
Generates audible bruits, thrills, and heart murmurs

steps.tx: The likelihood of flow transitioning from silent laminar streamlines to chaotic turbulence is calculated by the dimensionless **Reynolds number**. Reynolds number equals fluid velocity multiplied by vessel diameter and fluid density, divided by fluid viscosity. Values exceeding two thousand indicate high probability of turbulence, promoted by high blood velocity, wide vascular caliber, or severe anaemia.
steps.say: Reynolds number predicts turbulence: values over 2,000 favor turbulent flow, promoted by high velocity, large diameter, and low viscosity in anaemia.

rows: Flow acceleration through stenotic aortic valve
Hyperdynamic flow murmur in severe anaemia

steps.tx: In severe anaemia, a reduced red cell haematocrit lowers blood viscosity, accelerating cardiac output and blood velocity. Consequently, the Reynolds number surges, producing audible systolic **flow murmurs** over the precordium without structural valvular stenosis. Restoring haematocrit through blood transfusion elevates viscosity, reducing Reynolds number and silencing the murmur.
steps.say: In severe anaemia, reduced viscosity and compensatory high cardiac output drive Reynolds number over 2,000, producing benign systolic flow murmurs.

Whole Blood Viscosity Falls to Half of Normal Baseline

steps.tx: A critical physical law governing vessel wall stability is **Laplace law**. In a hollow cylindrical blood vessel, transmural distending pressure multiplied by internal vessel radius equals wall tension divided by wall thickness. In abdominal aortic aneurysms, chamber dilation increases radius, which escalates wall tension, predisposing the weakened dilated wall to catastrophic rupture.
steps.say: Laplace law dictates that wall tension rises with vessel radius. In aortic aneurysms, increasing diameter escalates wall tension, predisposing to rupture.

vis.caption: Aortic wall tension, post-stenotic turbulence, and Laplace law dynamics. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: When sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone increases markedly or perfusion pressure plummets, vascular smooth muscle tension overcomes internal distending blood pressure. The transmural pressure at which a microvessel collapses and blood flow ceases entirely is the **critical closing pressure**, normally measuring twenty millimetres of mercury but rising to sixty in intense sympathetic vasoconstriction.
steps.say: Critical closing pressure is the threshold where vessels collapse and flow stops completely, elevated during intense sympathetic vasoconstriction.

left.title: Normal Perfusion State
points: Transmural pressure exceeds active smooth muscle tone
Arteriolar and capillary lumens remain widely patent
Continuous capillary perfusion and solute clearance

right.title: Severe Vasoconstrictor State (Shock)
points: Intense sympathetic stimulation and noradrenaline surge
Active wall tension overcomes intravascular distending pressure
Microvessels snap closed, stopping capillary perfusion
Critical closing pressure shifts upward to 60 mmHg
